notes: Consent order on appeal; bankruptcy adjudication recorded without merits determination.

enrichment.short_title: Customs & Excise v Baars: consent order and bankruptcy without merits hearing
key_facts: Customs and Excise appealed against Jack Baars Wholesale and related respondents in a tax dispute.
The parties settled and agreed a form of order acceptable to Neuberger, Ward and Tuckey LJJ.
Certain appeals were allowed or dismissed without the Court determining the merits of any appeal or cross-appeal.
By consent the Court adjudicated Jack Baars bankrupt on 3 November 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal hearing at which the parties presented an agreed form of order following settlement.
enrichment.outcome: Order made substantially as agreed; Jack Baars adjudicated bankrupt; appeals resolved without merits determination.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties settle an appeal and agree a form of order, the Court may make the order without determining merits, provided the order fairly reflects the settlement and any statutory adjudication (such as bankruptcy) is properly recorded.
legal_issues: Whether appeals could be disposed of by consent without merits determination
Whether bankruptcy of a respondent could be adjudicated as part of the agreed order

confidence.notes: Very short judgment recording settlement and bankruptcy; limited substantive legal analysis.

notes: School exclusion JR; 16-day fixed-term exclusion for mooning upheld as not disproportionate.

enrichment.short_title: K v Tamworth Manor: challenge to 16-day exclusion for mooning on football pitch

statutes_considered.title: Education (Pupil Exclusions and Appeals) (Maintained Schools) (England) Regulations 2002

key_facts: The claimant was excluded for 16 days after truanting a maths lesson and mooning on a school football pitch during an inter-school match.
The head teacher and governors' discipline committee regarded the conduct as indecent, offensive and bringing the school into disrepute.
The claimant had a prior disciplinary record including earlier exclusions and internal sanctions in 2003.
Judicial review was permitted only on grounds that the penalty was unreasonable or disproportionate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a governors' decision upholding a head teacher's fixed-term exclusion exceeding 15 school days.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; section 39 anonymity extended to the claimant but not to the school; detailed assessment of costs ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Secretarial guidance suggesting 1–3 day exclusions is not a mandatory cap; a 16-day exclusion may be proportionate where mooning occurred before pupils and staff of another school and the pupil had a persistent disciplinary record.
legal_issues: Whether the governors failed to have regard to exclusion guidance as a material consideration
Whether a 16-day exclusion was disproportionate given paragraph 6.1 of the guidance
Whether the head teacher improperly used the 15-day threshold to trigger a governors' hearing

confidence.notes: Detailed fact findings and clear dismissal on proportionality grounds.

notes: Family appeal refusing permission to challenge MPS order including solicitors' costs.

enrichment.short_title: Minwalla: permission refused on solicitors' costs in maintenance pending suit
key_facts: Singer J ordered Mr Minwalla to pay about £8,000 per month maintenance pending suit, including sums to the wife's solicitors.
The husband paid only £3,250 and arrears approached £40,000; final ancillary relief was listed five months later.
The husband argued the judge had no jurisdiction to include monthly payments to the petitioner's solicitors in an MPS order.
The wife had incurred about £200,000 in costs with a projected total of £400,000; only a charged flat in Portland Place was within the jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Permission to appeal from an MPS order, listed orally after an adjournment application was refused on paper.
enrichment.outcome: Permission application dismissed; respondent ordered to pay costs to be assessed.
enrichment.ratio: Where an MPS order was of very short duration before final ancillary relief, non-payment had not been enforced, and the husband had brought an inappropriate appeal risking further costs, the Court of Appeal should refuse permission on grounds of proportionality even if a pure point of law merited consideration.
legal_issues: Whether maintenance pending suit may include monthly payments to the petitioner's solicitors
Whether A v A and G v G support such jurisdiction without Court of Appeal authority
Whether the appeal should be adjourned where the husband did not receive refusal of his adjournment application
linked_authorities: A v A (Maintenance Pending Suit: Solicitors' Costs) [2001] 1 FLR 377
G v G (Maintenance Pending Suit: Costs) [2003] 2 FLR 71

confidence.notes: Thorpe LJ's reasoning on jurisdiction and proportionality is explicit though the underlying MPS point remains undecided on appeal.

notes: Trade Descriptions Act prosecution quashed as oppressive abuse of process.

enrichment.short_title: R v Adaway: conservatory trade description prosecution stayed as oppressive
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Adaway traded as Quality Direct and installed a conservatory for Mr Byatt for about £18,000.
The conservatory lacked agreed roof vents and K glass in the sides; the roof glass dispute remained contested.
Mr Adaway was convicted on two counts of supplying goods with a false trade description; Mrs Adaway was acquitted on all counts.
Wokingham District Council prosecuted despite a trading standards officer initially considering civil resolution appropriate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge on abuse of process, inconsistent verdicts and summing-up grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions quashed; local authority ordered to pay defence and appeal costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a local authority's own enforcement policy required fraud or deliberate persistent breach and neither criterion was substantiated, refusal to stay an oppressive Trade Descriptions Act prosecution was a flawed exercise of discretion even if the judge later criticised the prosecution at sentence.
legal_issues: Whether the prosecution was an abuse of process under the council's Public Protection Enforcement Policy
Whether the judge erred in adopting a wait-and-see approach at the stay application
Whether jury verdicts on counts 1–2 versus count 3 were inconsistent
index_terms: Shropshire County Council v Simon Dudley
linked_authorities: Shropshire County Council v Simon Dudley Limited [1996] TLR 69

confidence.notes: Court found prosecution criteria wholly unsupported; detailed reasoning on policy and discretion.

notes: Administration application; BDO Stoy Hayward appointed over creditor's nominee.

enrichment.short_title: Re World Class Homes: appointment of administrators over creditor nominee
key_facts: Madison Advertising served a statutory demand and presented a winding-up petition against World Class Homes Limited.
The company applied for administration proposing BDO Stoy Hayward administrators; Madison proposed Jeremy Burman.
The company traded in Portuguese holiday property; BDO had begun gauging buyer interest before the hearing.
Creditor head-count and disclosure disputes favoured neither nominee decisively.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Contested administration application heard after interlocutory directions before Etherton J, with evidence on administrator choice.
enrichment.outcome: Administration order made appointing Geoffrey Stuart Kinman and Anthony John Sanderson of BDO Stoy Hayward; petitioner's costs as administration costs.
enrichment.ratio: On a contest between proposed administrators, existing acquaintance with the company's affairs and begun marketing efforts may outweigh a creditor's nominee where both are assumed independent; creditor canvassing and disclosure failures by the company do not necessarily taint the director's nominee.
legal_issues: Whether preconditions for administration under the Insolvency Act were satisfied
Whether creditor preference or loss of confidence in BDO Stoy Hayward should determine appointment
Application of Re Maxwell Communication Corporation guidance on administrator selection
linked_authorities: Re Maxwell Communication Corporation plc [1992] BCLC 465

confidence.notes: Lindsay J's appointment reasoning and Maxwell application are clearly stated.

notes: AG reference on firearms minimum sentence; section 5 count required; reference refused.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 114/2004: five-year minimum requires section 5 Firearms Act count
key_facts: A 23-year-old of previous good character pleaded guilty to possession of a converted blank-firing handgun with intent to cause fear of violence and two bladed articles.
He fired once outside a nightclub wearing a bullet-proof vest after retrieving the gun because of a gang dispute.
The judge sentenced him to three-and-a-half years, unaware the weapon was a prohibited weapon attracting a five-year minimum.
No section 5 possession count was included and prosecution did not seek to add one before sentence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging unduly lenient sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference refused; court held a section 5 count is required to trigger the statutory minimum and the overall sentence was within the proper range.
enrichment.ratio: The five-year minimum for possession of a prohibited weapon under section 287 of the 2003 Act requires a section 5 Firearms Act count or unequivocal admission; Benfield does not support triggering the minimum without such a count, and a sentence may fall within the judge's proper ambit even where aggravating features exist.
legal_issues: Whether the five-year minimum applies without a section 5 indictment count
Whether Benfield supports inferring prohibited-weapon possession from other counts
Whether three-and-a-half years was unduly lenient on the facts
linked_authorities: R v Benfield & Ors [2004] 1 Cr App R(S) 307
R v Avis [1998] 2 Cr App R(S) 178
Attorney-General's Reference No 4 of 1989 [1990] 11 Cr App R(S) 517

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of statutory minimum machinery and clear refusal of the reference.

notes: Rent review arbitration witness summonses set aside for drafting, necessity and confidentiality.

enrichment.short_title: South Tyneside v Wickes: set-aside of Acton letting witness summonses
key_facts: Tyneside and Wickes disputed open market rent on review of the Alperton lease, referred to arbitration.
Tyneside issued section 43 witness summonses against B&Q and Threadneedle for B&Q's Acton agreement-for-lease documents.
B&Q and Wickes were rival DIY bidders; the Acton agreement contained a confidentiality clause.
The original summonses were broadly drafted and sought extensive transaction documentation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court applications by non-parties B&Q and Mr Jordison to set aside witness summonses issued with arbitrator permission for a rent review arbitration.
enrichment.outcome: Witness summonses set aside; amended paragraph 1 alone permitted in drafting terms but applications succeeded on necessity and confidentiality.
enrichment.ratio: Witness summonses must identify documents specifically and not operate as disclosure; production is not necessary where other comparables exist and the landlord failed to seek Wickes's own Acton negotiation disclosure; acute commercial sensitivity and confidentiality in a rival-bidder context may justify setting aside even if a comparable letting is potentially relevant.
legal_issues: Whether the summonses were a fishing expedition or impermissible disclosure
Whether Acton documents were necessary for fair disposal of the rent review
Whether confidentiality and Cornwall Coast Country Club v Cardgrange rendered the transaction irrelevant
linked_authorities: Cornwall Coast Country Club v Cardgrange [1987] 1 EGLR 146
Lynall v Inland Revenue Commissioners [1972] AC 680
Land Securities plc v Westminster City Council [1993] 1 WLR 286

confidence.notes: Comprehensive judgment on witness summons principles and clear disposition on multiple grounds.

notes: Mid-trial amendments; Soilfrac mitigation quantum refused; extension credit permitted.

enrichment.short_title: Sainsbury v WSP: mid-trial pleading amendments at Newhaven supermarket
key_facts: Sainsbury claimed damages after defective ground-bearing slab design at a Newhaven supermarket caused settlement.
WSP had agreed to fund Keller Soilfrac remedial works; further settlement led Sainsbury to rebuild the store instead of requiring Keller's return.
On day four of trial WSP sought to quantify Soilfrac completion cost at £538,400 and extension foregone cost at £6.2 million.
The claimants objected that late amendments were irrelevant or prejudicial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Mid-trial applications for permission to amend defence and quantum statements and to strike parts of further information responses.
enrichment.outcome: Measure-of-loss amendment refused as irrelevant; extension credit amendment permitted; claimants' application to strike further information refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where mitigation required invoking Keller contract rights at WSP's expense such that Sainsbury would pay nothing, pleading an alternative measure of loss by Soilfrac completion cost is irrelevant to a failure-to-mitigate defence yielding nil recovery; extension credit amendments may be permitted late where based on the claimants' own Gleeds costing.
legal_issues: Whether £538,400 Soilfrac completion cost was a relevant measure of loss or mitigation
Whether £6.2 million extension credit amendment should be allowed mid-trial
Whether further information on abandoned extension plans should be struck out

confidence.notes: Clear mid-trial rulings with detailed factual and procedural context.

notes: Adjudication enforcement failed; June 2001 letter was letter of intent not JCT incorporation.

enrichment.short_title: Bryen & Langley v Boston: letter of intent did not incorporate JCT adjudication

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1999

key_facts: B&L began fitting-out works at Mrs Boston's New Cavendish Street flats on a June 2001 letter of intent from the quantity surveyor.
The letter contemplated a future JCT 1998 contract and early-start costs recovery if the project did not proceed; no JCT form was ever executed.
Interim certificate 11 left £65,995 unpaid; Mr Boston paid £50,000 but disputed any further liability.
An adjudicator determined the balance due; Mr Boston resisted summary enforcement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim and summary judgment application to enforce an adjudicator's decision on unpaid interim certificate balance.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment refused and action failed; adjudicator lacked jurisdiction because the contract did not incorporate JCT adjudication provisions.
enrichment.ratio: A letter stating the contract will be executed under JCT 1998 and that contract documents will be drawn up shortly is a preliminary letter of intent looking forward to a separate JCT contract, not an incorporation of the JCT form including clause 41A adjudication; without such incorporation a statutory or contractual adjudication scheme does not bind the employer.
legal_issues: Whether the 12 June 2001 letter incorporated the JCT form including adjudication
Whether adjudicator's jurisdiction decision was binding at enforcement
Whether JCT adjudication and withholding notice terms were unfair under the 1999 Regulations
linked_authorities: Director General of Fair Trading v First National Bank plc [2002] 1 AC 481
Lovell Projects Ltd v Legg and Carver [2003] 1 BLR 452
Westminster Building Co Ltd v Beckingham [2004] 1 BLR 265

confidence.notes: Detailed judgment on contract construction and extensive obiter on consumer regulations.

notes: AG reference; stepfather sexual abuse; community order replaced with 18 months.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 67/2004: unduly lenient community order for stepfather abuse
key_facts: A 69-year-old stepfather pleaded guilty to repeated indecent assaults on his stepson aged 6–12 and specimen offences against his stepdaughter.
Abuse included bath incidents, oral and manual masturbation on more than a hundred occasions, and touching the stepdaughter while their mother worked nights.
Both victims suffered lasting psychiatric harm; the offender had no previous convictions and low reoffending risk.
The Crown Court imposed a three-year community rehabilitation order with sex offender programme attendance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 alleging unduly lenient non-custodial sentence, adjourned for medical evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; community order quashed and replaced with 18 months' imprisonment concurrent on each offence, with surrender by noon the next day.
enrichment.ratio: Systematic breach of trust sexual abuse of two young stepchildren over years causing serious lasting harm warranted a significant custodial sentence; allowing for age, ill-health and double jeopardy, 18 months was the appropriate substituted term where the court below would properly have imposed about three years.
legal_issues: Whether a community rehabilitation order was unduly lenient for sustained intra-familial sexual abuse
Effect of offender age, health and double jeopardy on the substituted sentence
Application of Millberry and related Attorney General references
linked_authorities: R v Millberry & Ors [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 31
Attorney-General's Reference Nos 91, 119 and 120 of 2002 [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 338
Attorney-General's Reference No 5 of 2001 (R v Culshaw) [2001] 2 Cr App R(S) 473

confidence.notes: Full factual summary and explicit substituted sentence with double jeopardy reasoning.
